newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Woods applauds Biko breakthrough.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Woods applauds Biko breakthrough.

text.p: The man who first brought the world's attention to the death in detention of South African activist Steve Biko 19 years ago said on Tuesday he now hoped to finally hear the truth of his friend's last hours alive.

Donald Woods, a white newspaper editor who befriended Biko and wrote a 1978 biography of the black consciousness leader, applauded news that former white security policemen were ready to confess to killing Biko, in return for a pardon.
"It feels good, and the five names are very familiar to me," Woods said, referring to five policeman named by a newspaper.
"I've been wondering for years when they would come out of the woodwork," he told Reuters in an interview at his Johannesburg home.

"One remembers what a loss it was to the country, because he had such a gift of leadership and he could have fast-forwarded the process in solving the problems... He still left a powerful legacy," said Woods.
Biko died of brain damage in a Pretoria prison cell in September 1977 after he was driven naked in the back of a police van from Port Elizabeth, where he had been interrogated by security police.
He was the most prominent black activist to die while detained without trial under draconian security laws used to suppress opposition to apartheid.
Woods said bitterness was fruitless 19 years after Biko's death, and that his family and friends hoped only to finally learn the truth about the way he died.

"At least now we have a chance of finding out (the truth) whereas before there was nothing happening... I'm hoping it will lead to further revelations. Too much has been hidden for too long," he added.

Woods said he hoped Biko's interrogators would also admit knowledge of other police actions during the 1970s and 1980s in the Eastern Cape region aimed at crushing an internal revolt by blacks against apartheid.
"The Eastern Cape security police were particularly notorious and so I'm very glad that you finally can turn the spotlight on them."

Woods said he believed that Biko was brutally beaten when he bravely challenged the policemen interrogating him. He cited one other occasion when Biko -- surrounded by seven policemen -- was slapped by one of them. Biko slapped him back.

"There are very few human beings in this world who, alone in a prison cell with several people can fight back like that. So my guess has always been he said something to them which enraged them so much that they just lost it."

Biko and Woods were immortalised in Richard Attenborough's film Cry Freedom, based on the biography Woods wrote after he went into exile in Britain to escape police harassment, because of his friendship with Biko.
